1.pericope_label: The burden which Habakkuk the prophet did see
debates: Whether the burden falls on the Jews or on the Chaldeans
Why the title prophet is attached to this name
Whether the complaint is about present sin or coming invasion
outliers: Calvin dissents from the greater part of interpreters in referring the burden to the prophet own people
Ellicott leaves open whether the title marks membership of a prophetic college or simply an inspired minister
themes: A name that may mean embracing or being embraced
A prophecy without any of the usual formulas
A single word cried out as we cry fire
A man grieved by wrongs that were not his own

3.pericope_label: Why dost thou shew me iniquity, and cause me to behold grievance?
debates: Whose wickedness the prophet is complaining of
Whether such a complaint against God can be lawful
What the slackening of the law describes
outliers: Calvin defends the freedom of the complaint by asking what prayer is for, if not the unburdening of grief into the bosom of God
Gill prefers a rendering that makes the law intermittent, like a pulse too faint to be felt
themes: Wickedness done openly and without shame
Indignation counted a duty rather than a fault
Judgment that issues only for the wrong side
Anger easily kept for injuries of our own

5.pericope_label: Behold ye among the heathen, and regard, and wonder marvellously
debates: Whether the looking is addressed to the Jews or to the nations
Whether the received text or the Greek reading lies behind the apostolic quotation
Whether raising up the Chaldeans implies a newly risen nation
outliers: Ellicott denies that the apostolic citation gives any authority to the Greek variant, and doubts the apostle used it
Ellicott reports and rejects an ethnological theory that made these Chaldeans a lately arrived people
themes: Patience abused turning to a keen resentment
A punishment its own hearers would not credit
Pagans appointed as teachers to a taught people
A word twice repeated to raise alarm

7.pericope_label: They are terrible and dreadful: their judgment and their dignity shall proceed of themselves
debates: What it means that their judgment proceeds of themselves
How God can use cruel instruments without sharing their guilt
What the evening wolves stand for
outliers: Clarke alone reads the clause historically, of a nation made great by revolting from its overlord
Ellicott corrects the rendering of the wolves from more fierce to sharper
themes: Cruelty put to a use its owners never intended
Men who will not allow a judge over them
Horses unmoved by the roaring of a lion
A beast whose hunger sharpens toward evening

9.pericope_label: They shall come all for violence: their faces shall sup up as the east wind
debates: What the clause about their faces means
Why the invaders are said to come only for prey
What heaping dust describes
outliers: Ellicott rejects the east wind rendering on philological grounds despite granting that it gives a good sense
Calvin reads the ease of the conquest as evidence that God unnerves those who resist his word
themes: A wind that dries a man before he is out of the river
A word that occurs nowhere else in the book
Thrones filled and emptied at an invader pleasure
Walls climbed by heaping up dust

11.pericope_label: Then shall his mind change, and he shall pass over, and offend, imputing this his power unto his god
debates: What the changing of his mind describes
Whether the clause we shall not die is the true reading
Why the comfort is addressed to God rather than to the enemy
outliers: Ellicott abandons the received rendering and makes the verse a sudden anti-climax in which the conqueror is pronounced guilty at the height of his triumph
Clarke reports an emendation yielding God of truth and rejects it for want of manuscript support
themes: A disposition worsened by its own success
Promises spoken as if in private conference
Hard thoughts of God guarded against
A commission to correct but not to destroy

13.pericope_label: Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil, and canst not look on iniquity
debates: How this complaint differs from the one that opened the chapter
How God can be said not to look on iniquity when he sees everything
What the comparison with fishes charges God with
outliers: Calvin rejects an imperative rendering of the opening and reads the verse as two opposed halves, God nature against experience
Clarke answers the question outright by appealing to a mercy that suffers long
themes: A prophet pleading as an injured man rather than a zealot
Sight without approbation
A covenant people left as common as fish
A fisherman sacrificing to his own net

15.pericope_label: They take up all of them with the angle, they catch them in their net
debates: What the different fishing implements stand for
Whether the sacrifice to the net is literal worship or a figure
What the closing question actually asks
outliers: Calvin says all interpreters mistake the last verse, which asks not how soon the net is cast again but whether it is ever to be cast
Ellicott illustrates the figure from a modern nation said to have worshipped a new weapon as a goddess
themes: Covenants and tribute used as bait
A warrior invoking his own right hand
Success mistaken for a verdict of justice
A hunter made keener by every capture
